Reproducing Raicevic et al. (2023) from dandiset 000491¶

Paper. Raicevic N, Forer JM, Ladrón-de-Guevara A, Du T, Nedergaard M, Kelley DH, Boster K (2023). Sizes and shapes of perivascular spaces surrounding murine pial arteries. Research Square preprint, version 1, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-2587250/v1. The claims file was written from the full text of this preprint as served by PubMed Central (PMC9949243), with its figure legends and Tables 1 to 3; the Additional Files were not in the text. The paper links no code.

Dandiset. DANDI:000491, version 0.230602.1307 (doi:10.48324/dandi.000491/0.230602.1307). The paper cites no version. This is the most recent published version, and the only one that can support the analysis: the earlier version 0.230427.1809 holds no PVS mask for locations L, M and N (the data check below lists the masks each version holds). The draft has the same 14 assets and size.

What the dandiset holds. For each of the 14 pial artery segments (locations A to N, 9 mice), the 3D two-photon stack and the final binary segmentations of the vessel and of the PVS. The 2D time series used to validate the segmentation are not in it. Everything here starts from the deposited segmentations, as the claims file says; the paper's segmentation includes manual steps that cannot be redone.

Method. The pipeline P1 to P9 of the claims file's opening comment, in pvs.py: isotropic sampling, a 3D skeleton of the vessel cleaned of erroneous points, second-order polynomial fits of the centerline, normal cross sections, the PVS lobes beside the vessel in each, the edge exclusion from the vessel center, areas, the circle fit of the vessel, the ellipse, spline and polynomial fits, and the hydraulic resistance by a finite-difference solution of the Poisson equation (in place of MATLAB's finite elements). Every reading the claims file names is run, with one exception stated in the attempt record: reading (b) of P2 (all skeleton points, 10^4 to 10^5 per segment) is run for the counts only. No random numbers are used.

Revision after the first verification. The verifier found the longest path through the skeleton much longer than the vessel (it runs into branches and doubles back) and the PVS of a cross section taken over the whole plane. The path is now cleaned of erroneous points, the PVS of a cross section is the two largest PVS regions beside the vessel, planes that the PVS mask fills edge to edge (E and F) are cleared, and the edge distance is measured from the vessel center in the slice. The data check shows the path before and after cleaning, the PVS content of the cross sections and one cross section per location with the fits drawn over it.

Revision after the second verification. The data check shows how far the cleaned path still meanders, cross-section-counts adds the counts a path along the fitted centerline would give, and a cell before the summary computes every claim's table again without location E, whose cleaned path follows a side branch. Statements the verifier found unsupported are corrected.

Third verification. The verifier reviewed the proposed change of cross-section-counts to reproduced and did not agree; the outcome stays not reproduced.

Answer from a reader. A question on fig8-ellipse-parameters asked whether the ellipse fit is the PVS's alone or that of the PVS and vessel together. The reader amended the claims file (questions/000491.yaml): the ellipse is now fit to the region the PVS's outer boundary encloses, the PVS and vessel segmentations together with holes filled, for every claim that uses it (fig5d, table2, fig5b, ellipse-annulus-underestimate, fig7 and fig8). This notebook uses that ellipse; the ellipse of the PVS alone is shown as a variant under fig8.

Run time. About 29 minutes on four cores, almost all in the cross sections and the resistance solves.

Data check¶

Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output. The stacks are static 3D images, with no time base and no trial table, so there is no clock to align; the check that matters here is the geometry (voxel size, depth direction, which mask is which).

In [2]:
def depth_offset(ves, pv):
    """Per (y, x) column holding both masks, the PVS's mean plane minus the vessel's mean plane."""
    z = np.arange(ves.shape[0])[:, None, None]
    vz = (z * ves).sum(0) / np.maximum(ves.sum(0), 1)
    pz = (z * pv).sum(0) / np.maximum(pv.sum(0), 1)
    both = ves.any(0) & pv.any(0)
    return (pz - vz)[both]


rows = []
for a in assets:
    f = pvs.open_asset(a)
    ves, pv = pvs.load_masks(f)
    vx = pvs.voxel_size(f)
    zv = np.nonzero(ves.any((1, 2)))[0]
    zp = np.nonzero(pv.any((1, 2)))[0]
    acq = f["acquisition"]
    # vessel intensity against depth, on 8 planes through the vessel (ChanA, the vessel channel)
    d = acq["TwoPhotonSeriesChanA/data"]
    zs = np.linspace(zv[0], zv[-1], 8).astype(int)
    prof = [float(d[z, :, :, 0][ves[z]].mean()) for z in zs]
    rho = stats.spearmanr(zs, prof).statistic
    rows.append({
        "location": pvs.location_of(f), "subject": f["general/subject/subject_id"][()].decode(),
        "strain": f["general/subject/strain"][()].decode(), "sex": f["general/subject/sex"][()].decode(),
        "age": f["general/subject/age"][()].decode(), "planes": ves.shape[0], "shape_yx": ves.shape[1:],
        "voxel_um": vx, "channels": ",".join(k[-1] for k in acq), "image_dtype": str(d.dtype),
        "masks": ",".join(k[-1] for k in f["processing/ophys/ImageSegmentation"]),
        "vessel_vox": int(ves.sum()), "pvs_vox": int(pv.sum()), "overlap_vox": int((ves & pv).sum()),
        "pvs_frac_volume": round(pv.mean(), 3), "vessel_z": (int(zv[0]), int(zv[-1])),
        "pvs_z": (int(zp[0]), int(zp[-1])), "deepest_plane_pvs_frac": round(pv[zp[-1]].mean(), 2),
        "intensity_vs_depth_rho": round(rho, 2),
        # whole-plane mean intensity of every channel against depth (every 4th pixel), same planes
        "plane_rho_by_channel": {k[-1]: round(stats.spearmanr(zs, [float(np.asarray(acq[k]["data"][z, ::4, ::4, 0]).mean())
                                                                   for z in zs]).statistic, 2) for k in sorted(acq)},
        "planes_over_90pct_pvs": int((pv.mean((1, 2)) > pvs.FILLED_PLANE).sum()),
        # depth of the PVS against the vessel, in columns holding both, after clearing filled planes

        "emission_nm": [float(f[f"general/optophysiology/{p}/optical_channel/emission_lambda"][()])
                        for p in f["general/optophysiology"]],
    })

Checks of the metadata against the values:

  • Nine subjects and 14 files, one per location, as the description maps them. Every file has a vessel mask (ChanA) and a PVS mask (ChanC). Image channels are float64 in "arbitrary unit".
  • Depth direction. The mean vessel-channel intensity inside the vessel mask falls with plane index in most files (negative rank correlation above), as the Methods expect from attenuation with depth, so plane 0 is the surface side. This is consistent with, not proof of, the orientation.
  • Location D, the one file where the intensity inside the vessel rises with plane index. The mean intensity over the whole plane falls with plane index in all its channels (plane_rho_by_channel), as in the other files, and its PVS lies above the vessel (negative pvs_minus_vessel_depth_planes), as in every file but E and F. So plane 0 is taken as the surface side in D too; the rise inside its vessel mask does not by itself show a reversed depth axis.
  • The PVS mask fills whole planes in E and F (planes_over_90pct_pvs: every plane below a depth); no plane of any other file is more than half PVS. These planes are cleared before the cross sections are taken (pvs.clear_filled_planes, an assumption stated in the attempt record).
  • Overlap: the Methods say overlaps between the vessel and PVS segmentations were removed by hand; the deposited masks still overlap in most files (overlap_vox).
  • Emission wavelengths: the file gives 698 nm for ChanA, described as FITC-dextran, and 525 nm for ChanC, the PVS tracer; the Methods say the green (525 nm) channel holds the FITC-dextran.

# Voxel size in depth. L, M and N state 0.648 um per plane, the others 1 um, while every session
# description says the planes are 1 um apart. A pial artery is close to round in cross section,
# so the height-to-width ratio of the vessel in the normal cross sections tests the stated depth.
d = DATA["a"]
d = d[d.keep_b & (d.ves_area > 0)]
rnd = d.assign(hw=d.ves_h / d.ves_w).groupby("location").hw.median()
print("Median vessel height / width in normal cross sections, with each file's stated voxel depth:")
print(pd.DataFrame({"height_over_width": rnd.round(2), "stated_dz_um": info.voxel_um.map(lambda v: v[2])}).to_string())
print("\nDigests of the masks (duplicate recordings would share one):")
dig = META["a"].digest
print("distinct:", dig.nunique(), "of", len(dig))
# Versions: what each published version holds
for v in ("0.230427.1809", pvs.VERSION):
    held = {}
    for a in pvs.list_assets(v):
        f = pvs.open_asset(a)
        held[pvs.location_of(f)] = ",".join(k[-1] for k in f["processing/ophys/ImageSegmentation"])
    print(f"version {v}: masks per location", dict(sorted(held.items())))

If the depth were mis-stated by the ratio 1 / 0.648, the vessel in those files would look 1.54 times taller or shorter than wide. The ratios above say whether the stated voxel sizes are consistent with round vessels. The earlier published version lacks the PVS masks of L, M and N, so it cannot support the analysis; the pinned version holds all 14.

def sel(p1, p4):
    d = DATA[p1]
    return d[d["keep_" + p4]]


def ratio_seg(d, p5, k=3):
    """Segmentation area ratio: P5 reading a, segmented vessel area; b, the fitted circle."""
    return d.pvs_area / (d.ves_area if p5 == "a" else np.pi * d[f"R1_e{k}"] ** 2)


def within(x, value, tol):
    return bool(np.isfinite(x) and abs(x - value) <= tol + 1e-12)


d = sel("a", "b")
share = d.overlap_area / (d.pvs_area + d.overlap_area)
print("Pixels in both masks, as a share of the PVS mask in each slice (P1 a, P4 b): median",
      round(share.median(), 4), "; slices above 5%:", int((share > 0.05).sum()), "of", len(d), "; by location above 5%:",
      share.gt(0.05).groupby(d.location).sum().to_dict())

Centerline and PVS content of the cross sections¶

The verifier of round 1 found the longest path through the skeleton longer than any straight line through the volume, and the PVS of a slice taken over the whole 332 um plane. The path is now cleaned of erroneous points (pvs.clean_path: points farther from the polynomial fit than the vessel radius, and points that revisit a stretch already passed), the PVS of a slice is the two largest PVS regions within one vessel radius of the vessel (pvs.pvs_lobes), and the edge distance of P4 is measured from the vessel center found in the slice, to which the paper shifts the slice. The tables below show the path before and after cleaning, the PVS content of the kept cross sections, and one cross section per location with the fits drawn over it.

Before cleaning, the longest path is 1.28 to 2.24 times the straight distance between its ends at 0.648 um (1.22 to 2.23 at 1 um), as the verifier found. Cleaning keeps 7534 of 9564 points (4974 of 6010 at 1 um), and the mean step between neighbouring kept points is 0.83 to 0.93 um at 0.648 um. The cleaned path still meanders: at 0.648 um its length (kept points times the mean step) is 1.13 to 1.78 times the distance between its kept ends and 1.08 to 1.44 times the arc of the fitted centerline at every location but E (0.91 there, where the gaps between kept points make that product shorter than the path). A 26-connected path along a straight line is at most about 8% longer than the line, so most of the excess is the path meandering inside the vessel, not the zigzag of the voxels. The vessel mask of E holds a network of branching vessels, which the Methods say were removed by hand; its cleaned path keeps 361 of 939 points along a side branch (right of the projection), while the points removed run along the vessel with PVS beside it (left). E's cross sections are therefore of the branch. Its median R1 is the largest of the 14 locations (40.9 um, under vessel-radius-peak); the paper gives no per-location radii to compare with. By median area, the PVS lobes kept are 91 to 99% of the slice's PVS pixels at every location but E (52% at 0.648 um, 29% at 1 um; the rest is the band left above the cleared planes and the PVS of other vessels) and, at 1 um, H (70%). The lobes are wide: by median, 48 to 72% of their area lies within 3 R1 of the vessel center at B, D, E and G, and 77 to 100% elsewhere. At F the lobes still join a band of PVS along the bottom of the slice (the example above). Measuring the edge distance from the vessel center moves it by 0.75 to 3.85 um by median and keeps 6683 cross sections in place of 6665 (P1 a, P4 b). The effect of E on each claim is shown before the summary.

cross-section-counts¶

After excluding cross sections near the edge of the imaging volume, each of the 14 PVS segments yields between 54 and 451 normal cross sections, about 0.8 um apart.

Every combination of P1 (voxel 0.648 or 1 um), P2 (longest path or all skeleton points) and P4 (median width from the horizontal extent of the PVS, or from the polynomial fit). Holds when the fewest and most per segment lie in 48.6 to 496.1 and the mean spacing is 0.72 to 0.88 um.

rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        g = DATA[p1].groupby("location")["keep_" + p4].sum()
        sp = META[p1].spacing.mean()
        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P2": "a", "P4": p4, "fewest": int(g.min()), "most": int(g.max()),
                     "segments_with_0": int((g == 0).sum()), "mean_spacing_um": round(sp, 3)})
    for p4 in P4:
        n = []
        for r in COUNTS_B[p1]:
            med = r["med_hext"] if p4 == "a" else r["med_wpol"]
            n.append(int((r["edge_dist"] >= med / 2.5).sum()))
        sp = np.mean([r["spacing"] for r in COUNTS_B[p1]])
        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P2": "b", "P4": p4, "fewest": min(n), "most": max(n),
                     "segments_with_0": sum(x == 0 for x in n), "mean_spacing_um": round(sp, 3)})
cc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
cc["counts_in_range"] = (cc.fewest >= 54 - 5.4) & (cc.most <= 451 + 45.1)
cc["spacing_ok"] = (cc.mean_spacing_um - 0.8).abs() <= 0.08
cc["holds"] = cc.counts_in_range & cc.spacing_ok
print(cc.to_string(index=False))
print("\nPer location, P2 a (path order spacing in um):")
print(pd.concat({p1: META[p1][["points", "spacing"]].round(3) for p1 in TARGET}, axis=1).to_string())
print("\nP2 b points per location:", {p1: {r["location"]: r["n_points"] for r in COUNTS_B[p1]} for p1 in TARGET})

# Path meander (data check): the counts a path without meander would give, at the same mean step
# along the fitted centerline, with the same share of cross sections kept under P4 b. A diagnostic,
# not a reading of the claims file, which takes one slice per centerline point.
est = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    g = DATA[p1].groupby("location").keep_b.sum()
    n_fit = (MEANDER[p1].fit_arc_um / META[p1].spacing).reindex(g.index)
    kept = (g / META[p1].points * n_fit).round().astype(int)
    est.append({"P1": p1, "P4": "b", "step_um": "path mean", "fewest": int(kept.min()), "most": int(kept.max()),
                "mean_spacing_um": round(META[p1].spacing.mean(), 3),
                "counts_in_range": bool(kept.min() >= 54 - 5.4 and kept.max() <= 451 + 45.1), "per_location": kept.to_dict()})
    # the same at the paper's 0.8 um and at the bounds of the spacing tolerance
    for st in (0.72, 0.8, 0.88):
        k_st = (g / META[p1].points * MEANDER[p1].fit_arc_um.reindex(g.index) / st).round().astype(int)
        est.append({"P1": p1, "P4": "b", "step_um": st, "fewest": int(k_st.min()), "most": int(k_st.max()), "mean_spacing_um": st,
                    "counts_in_range": bool(k_st.min() >= 54 - 5.4 and k_st.max() <= 451 + 45.1), "per_location": ""})
print("\nDiagnostic, counts along the fitted centerline at a given step (P4 b):")
print(pd.DataFrame(est).to_string(index=False))

Result: not reproduced. No combination of P1, P2 and P4 holds. With the cleaned path (P2 a) and the polynomial width (P4 b), the segments give 202 to 604 cross sections at 0.648 um, with a mean spacing of 0.876 um (within tolerance) but the most above 496.1, and 124 to 394 at 1 um, inside the range widened by 10%, but with a mean spacing of 1.345 um. With the horizontal extent of the PVS (P4 a), 4 segments keep no cross section at either voxel size. All skeleton points (P2 b) give up to 78712 per segment at 0.648 um and 36106 at 1 um.

The cleaned path still meanders (data check), so it holds more points than a path along the vessel would. As a diagnostic, not a reading of the claims file, counted along the fitted centerline at each segment's own mean step and with the share kept under P4 (b), the segments would give 223 to 427 cross sections at 0.648 um, with the mean spacing of 0.876 um, which meets the criterion (134 to 282 at 1 um, where the spacing stays 1.345 um). The count depends on the step a path along the vessel would have: at the paper's 0.8 um it is 241 to 492, inside 48.6 to 496.1; at 0.88 um 219 to 447; at 0.72 um 267 to 546, above it. So at 0.648 um the claim would hold with a path along the vessel at a step of 0.8 um or more, and the outcome turns on how the path is cleaned, which is an assumption. The attempt record proposed a change to reproduced. The third verification did not agree: these counts are scaled from the kept share, not taken from slices along a path that follows the vessel, that path is a reading outside the claims file, and the step of 0.876 um is the mean step of the meandering path, not one measured along the vessel (an average 26-connected step of about 0.73 um would give a most of about 539). The outcome stays not reproduced.

fig5a-pvs-area-scales-with-vessel-area¶

PVS area increases with vessel area only approximately; the least-squares line of PVS area on vessel area over all cross sections has slope 1.05 (95% CI 0.973 to 1.12) and R2 of 0.158.

Ordinary least squares on the segmented areas of every retained cross section, (a) with an intercept, (b) through the origin. Slope within 0.077 of 1.05 and R2 within 0.0158 of 0.158. R2 through the origin is computed against the mean (centred), so that it is comparable with (a); the uncentred value is also shown.

In [7]:
rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        x, y = d.ves_area.values, d.pvs_area.values
        r = stats.linregress(x, y)
        tq = stats.t.ppf(0.975, len(x) - 2)
        b0 = (x @ y) / (x @ x)
        res = y - b0 * x
        se0 = np.sqrt(res @ res / (len(x) - 1) / (x @ x))
        r2c = 1 - (res @ res) / ((y - y.mean()) @ (y - y.mean()))
        r2u = 1 - (res @ res) / (y @ y)
        for rd, slope, lo, hi, r2 in (("a", r.slope, r.slope - tq * r.stderr, r.slope + tq * r.stderr, r.rvalue ** 2),
                                      ("b", b0, b0 - tq * se0, b0 + tq * se0, r2c)):
            rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "reading": rd, "n": len(x), "slope": round(slope, 3),
                         "ci_low": round(lo, 3), "ci_high": round(hi, 3), "R2": round(r2, 3),
                         "R2_uncentred": round(r2u, 3) if rd == "b" else np.nan,
                         "intercept_um2": round(r.intercept, 1) if rd == "a" else 0.0,
                         "match": within(slope, 1.05, 0.077) and within(r2, 0.158, 0.0158)})
f5a = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f5a.to_string(index=False))

area-ratio-per-location¶

The peak of the segmented area ratio distribution ranges from 0.6 to 11.43 across the 14 locations, and in all but one location the ratio's variation along the vessel lies within 30% of the peak, so variation between segments dominates.

Per location, P5 and P7 as above. "Within 30% of the peak": (a) the 25th and 75th percentiles both lie within 30% of the peak; (b) IQR at most 30% of the peak; (c) IQR at most 60% of the peak; (d) all non-outlier values within 30% of the peak. Expected: smallest peak 0.54 to 0.66, largest 10.29 to 12.57, count of locations 11.7 to 14.3.

In [10]:
def per_location_peaks(d, values, p7, frac, readings):
    out = []
    for loc, v in values.groupby(d.location):
        v = v.replace([np.inf], np.nan).dropna()
        if len(v) < 5:
            continue
        pk = pvs.peak(v, p7)
        q25, q75 = np.percentile(v, [25, 75])
        nof = pvs.outlier_free(v)
        r = {"location": loc, "n": len(v), "peak": pk, "q25": q25, "q75": q75,
             "a": (abs(q25 - pk) <= frac * pk) and (abs(q75 - pk) <= frac * pk),
             "b": (q75 - q25) <= frac * pk, "c": (q75 - q25) <= 2 * frac * pk,
             "d": bool(np.all(np.abs(nof - pk) <= frac * pk))}
        out.append({k: r[k] for k in ["location", "n", "peak", "q25", "q75"] + list(readings)})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

fig5d-polynomial-closest-area-ratio¶

Of the three fits, the polynomial fit matches the segmentation's area ratio most closely in 73% of cross sections, the spline fit in 19% and the ellipse fit in 8%, and its distribution matches the segmentation's best.

Per cross section, the fit whose area ratio is closest to the segmentation's. Every combination of P5 (for the segmentation and, separately, for the fits), P6 and P9 (ellipse region a, ellipse minus its overlap with the circle; b, ellipse area minus circle area), under each P1 and P4. Only cross sections where all three fits exist are counted. Shares within 7.3, 1.9 and 0.8 points of 73, 19 and 8%.

In [11]:
def fit_ratios(d, k, p5_fit, p9):
    den = np.pi * d[f"R1_e{k}"] ** 2 if p5_fit == "a" else d.ves_area
    ell = d[f"ell_area_a_e{k}"] if p9 == "a" else d[f"ell_area_b_e{k}"]
    return pd.DataFrame({"polynomial": d[f"pol_area_e{k}"] / den, "spline": d[f"spl_area_e{k}"] / den,
                         "ellipse": ell / den})


rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            for p5s in "ab":
                seg = ratio_seg(d, p5s, k)
                for p5f in "ab":
                    for p9 in "ab":
                        fr = fit_ratios(d, k, p5f, p9)
                        ok = fr.notna().all(axis=1) & np.isfinite(seg)
                        best = (fr[ok].sub(seg[ok], axis=0)).abs().idxmin(axis=1)
                        sh = best.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(["polynomial", "spline", "ellipse"]).fillna(0) * 100
                        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P5_seg": p5s, "P5_fit": p5f, "P9": p9, "n": int(ok.sum()),
                                     "dropped": int((~ok).sum()), **sh.round(1).to_dict(),
                                     "match": within(sh.polynomial, 73, 7.3) and within(sh.spline, 19, 1.9) and within(sh.ellipse, 8, 0.8),
                                     "partial": sh.polynomial == sh.max() and sh.polynomial > 50})
f5d = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f5d.to_string(index=False))
print("\nCombinations matching:", int(f5d.match.sum()), "; meeting the partial rule:", int(f5d.partial.sum()), "of", len(f5d))

Result: reproduced. Four of the 96 combinations put the three shares within tolerance, all with P4 (b), the segmented vessel area for the segmentation's ratio and the fitted circle for the fits: P1 (a) with erosion 5 (polynomial 70.7%, spline 20.6%, ellipse 8.8% with P9 a; 70.4, 20.8 and 8.8% with P9 b) and P1 (b) with erosion 3 (71.4, 20.8 and 7.9%; 71.0, 20.8 and 8.3%). The polynomial share is the largest and above 50% in 92 of the 96 combinations, and runs from 47.4 to 79.1% over all. The outcome rests on those four; under the other readings of P5 the ellipse is closest in only 0.1 to 4.7% of cross sections.

table2-fit-area-ratio-peaks¶

The area ratio distribution peaks at 1.21 for the polynomial fit (close to the segmentation's 1.12), 2.08 for the ellipse fit, which does not narrow at the ends, and 1.48 for the spline fit, whose ratio varies little because it scales with vessel size alone.

Peaks, medians and the spline IQR of the fits' area ratios under each reading of P5 for the fits, P6, P7, P9 (ellipse region), P1 and P4.

                    for p7 in P7:
                        v = {"pk_pol": pvs.peak(fr.polynomial.dropna(), p7), "pk_ell": pvs.peak(fr.ellipse.dropna(), p7),
                             "pk_spl": pvs.peak(fr.spline.dropna(), p7), "md_pol": fr.polynomial.median(),
                             "md_ell": fr.ellipse.median(), "md_spl": fr.spline.median(), "iqr_spl": iqr["spline"]}
                        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P5_fit": p5f, "P9": p9, "P7": p7,
                                     **{n: round(x, 3) for n, x in v.items()},
                                     "iqr_pol": round(iqr["polynomial"], 3), "iqr_ell": round(iqr["ellipse"], 3),
                                     "n_within": sum(within(v[n], e, t) for n, e, t in EXP_T2),
                                     "match": all(within(v[n], e, t) for n, e, t in EXP_T2),
                                     "partial": (v["pk_ell"] > v["pk_spl"] > v["pk_pol"]) and iqr["spline"] < min(iqr["polynomial"], iqr["ellipse"])})
t2 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(t2.to_string(index=False))
print("\nCombinations meeting the partial rule:")
print(t2[t2.partial].to_string(index=False))
print("\nCombinations matching:", int(t2.match.sum()), "; meeting the partial rule:", int(t2.partial.sum()), "of", len(t2),
      "; most values within tolerance in one combination:", int(t2.n_within.max()), "of 7")
print("\nThe 8 combinations with the most values within tolerance (compact):")
print(t2.sort_values("n_within", ascending=False).head(8)[["P1", "P4", "P6", "P5_fit", "P9", "P7"] + [n for n, _, _ in EXP_T2] + ["n_within"]].to_string(index=False))
print("Ranges over all combinations:", {n: (t2[n].min(), t2[n].max()) for n, _, _ in EXP_T2})

Over all combinations the polynomial peak is 0.842 to 12.237 (expected 1.21), the ellipse peak 0.682 to 14.544 (2.08) and the spline peak 1.47 to 1.897 (1.48); the medians are 1.467 to 1.85 (2.15), 1.848 to 2.455 (2.89) and 1.504 to 1.71 (1.58), and the spline IQR is 0.019 to 0.26 (0.3). The spline's ratio is nearly constant, as the paper says.

fig6a-resistance-power-law¶

The hydraulic resistance per unit length of the segmented PVS is well predicted by a power law in PVS area (R2 = 0.944), with exponent -1.75 (95% CI -1.763 to -1.737), close to the -2 of a shape scaled in size alone.

Readings: (a) least squares of log resistance on log area, R2 on the log scale; (b) nonlinear least squares of resistance on area, R2 on the linear scale. Exponent within 0.013 of -1.75, R2 within 0.0944 of 0.944. The solver check of P8 (a circle of the same area within 1% of the exact resistance) is shown first.

In [13]:
# Solver check (Methods, Hydraulic resistance): circles of the areas met here
chk = []
for p1, px in TARGET.items():
    for area_um2 in (300, 1000, 3000, 10000):
        rpx = np.sqrt(area_um2 / np.pi) / px
        n = int(2 * rpx + 20)
        m = pvs.disk((n, n), n / 2, n / 2, rpx)
        R, _, _ = pvs.poiseuille(m, px)
        a = (np.sqrt(m.sum() / np.pi) - 1.5) * px * 1e-6  # the domain: 1.5 pixels inside the mask
        chk.append({"P1": p1, "area_um2": area_um2, "error_vs_exact": round(R / (8 * pvs.MU / (np.pi * a ** 4)) - 1, 4)})
print(pd.DataFrame(chk).to_string(index=False))
d = sel("a", "b")
eq_r = np.sqrt(d.pvs_area / np.pi)
print("Median PVS area", round(d.pvs_area.median()), "um^2; median radius of the circle of the same area", round(eq_r.median(), 1), "um")

rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        ok = np.isfinite(d.R_seg) & (d.R_seg > 0) & (d.pvs_area > 0)
        A, R = d.pvs_area[ok].values * 1e-12, d.R_seg[ok].values
        r = stats.linregress(np.log(A), np.log(R))
        tq = stats.t.ppf(0.975, len(A) - 2)
        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "reading": "a", "n": len(A), "exponent": round(r.slope, 4),
                     "ci_low": round(r.slope - tq * r.stderr, 4), "ci_high": round(r.slope + tq * r.stderr, 4),
                     "R2": round(r.rvalue ** 2, 4), "match": within(r.slope, -1.75, 0.013) and within(r.rvalue ** 2, 0.944, 0.0944),
                     "partial": within(r.rvalue ** 2, 0.944, 0.0944) and -2 <= r.slope <= -1.5})
        pp, cov = curve_fit(lambda a, c, k: c * a ** k, A / A.mean(), R / R.mean(), p0=(1, r.slope), maxfev=20000)
        pred = pp[0] * (A / A.mean()) ** pp[1] * R.mean()
        r2 = 1 - np.sum((R - pred) ** 2) / np.sum((R - R.mean()) ** 2)
        se = np.sqrt(cov[1, 1])
        rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "reading": "b", "n": len(A), "exponent": round(pp[1], 4),
                     "ci_low": round(pp[1] - 1.96 * se, 4), "ci_high": round(pp[1] + 1.96 * se, 4), "R2": round(r2, 4),
                     "match": within(pp[1], -1.75, 0.013) and within(r2, 0.944, 0.0944),
                     "partial": within(r2, 0.944, 0.0944) and -2 <= pp[1] <= -1.5})
f6a = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f6a.to_string(index=False))

Result: partially reproduced. No combination gives the exponent within 0.013 of -1.75. The log-log fit (reading a) gives -1.926 to -2.039 with R2 0.911 to 0.944, and two combinations meet the partial rule (R2 within tolerance, exponent between -2 and -1.5): P1 (a), P4 (a), exponent -1.977 (95% CI -1.993 to -1.961) and R2 0.944, and P1 (a), P4 (b), -1.926 (-1.939 to -1.912) and R2 0.922. The nonlinear fit (reading b) gives -2.99 to -4.69; a few cross sections with very large resistance (up to 1.88e21 Pa s/m^4) dominate it, so it says little about the power law. The solver is within 2.5% of the exact resistance for circles of 300 to 10000 um^2 (within 1% from 1000 um^2). Per-location exponents (P1 a, P4 b) run from -2.89 (B) to -1.315 (D); they are not computed for C, E, I and J, which hold cross sections with no flow domain.

The peak is within tolerance (1.557e15 to 1.903e15) in three combinations: 1.86e15 Pa s/m^4 with P1 (a), P4 (a), all values and logarithmic bins; 1.68e15 with P1 (a), P4 (b), outliers out and linear bins; and 1.83e15 with P1 (b), P4 (b), outliers out and linear bins. The median is 5.28e15 to 6.87e15 in every combination, against 3.84e15 within 3.84e14. The partial rule needs the median within tolerance, so neither the claim nor its partial rule holds.

fig5b-polynomial-closest-resistance¶

The distribution of hydraulic resistance of the polynomial fit matches that of the segmentation most closely, followed by the ellipse fit, and the polynomial fit is the best match for the majority of cross sections; the distribution peaks are 1.44e15 (polynomial), 7.06e14 (ellipse), 1.07e16 (spline) and 1.32e15 (optimal annulus) Pa s/m^4.

The fits' resistances are solved with the circle fit of each erosion of P6. The annulus follows Equation 3 as the claims file reads it, with K the segmentation's area ratio (P5 a or b) and R1 of the same erosion. Competing models: (a) the three fits, (b) the fits and the annulus. Peaks on linear bins (P7); the logarithmic bins are shown as a variant.

In [16]:
def models(d, p5, k=3):
    K = ratio_seg(d, p5, k)
    return pd.DataFrame({"segmentation": d.R_seg, "polynomial": d[f"R_pol_e{k}"], "ellipse": d[f"R_ell_e{k}"],
                         "spline": d[f"R_spl_e{k}"], "annulus": pvs.optimal_annulus(K, d[f"R1_e{k}"] * 1e-6)}
                        ).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)


EXP_PK = {"polynomial": (1.44e15, 1.44e14), "ellipse": (7.06e14, 7.06e13), "spline": (1.07e16, 1.07e15), "annulus": (1.32e15, 1.32e14)}
rows, rows_v = [], []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k, p5 in [(k, p5) for k in P6 for p5 in "ab"]:
            M = models(d, p5, k)
            ok = M.notna().all(axis=1)
            M = M[ok]
            for comp, names in (("a", ["polynomial", "ellipse", "spline"]), ("b", ["polynomial", "ellipse", "spline", "annulus"])):
                best = M[names].sub(M.segmentation, axis=0).abs().idxmin(axis=1).value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(names).fillna(0) * 100
                for p7 in P7:
                    for sc in ("linear", "log"):
                        pk = {n: rpeak(M[n], p7, sc) for n in ["segmentation"] + list(EXP_PK)}
                        r = {"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P5": p5, "models": comp, "P7": p7, "bins": sc, "n": len(M), "dropped": int((~ok).sum()),
                             **{f"best_{n[:4]}": round(best.get(n, np.nan), 1) for n in ["polynomial", "ellipse", "spline", "annulus"]},
                             **{f"pk_{n[:4]}": f"{pk[n]:.3g}" for n in pk},
                             "peaks_within": sum(within(pk[n], *EXP_PK[n]) for n in EXP_PK)}
                        r["match"] = best["polynomial"] > 50 and r["peaks_within"] == 4
                        r["partial"] = best["polynomial"] == best.max()
                        (rows if sc == "linear" else rows_v).append(r)
f5b = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f5b.to_string(index=False))
print("\nVariant, logarithmic bins (not part of the criterion):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows_v).to_string(index=False))
print("\nSummary by competing models (linear bins): polynomial best-match share and peaks within tolerance")
print(f5b.groupby("models").agg(best_poly_min=("best_poly", "min"), best_poly_max=("best_poly", "max"),
                                 partial=("partial", "sum"), combos=("partial", "size"), peaks_within_max=("peaks_within", "max")).to_string())
M = models(sel("a", "b"), "a")
print("\nMedian resistance by model (P1 a, P4 b, P5 a):", {c: f"{M[c].median():.3g}" for c in M})

      {c: round(stats.ks_2samp(M[c].dropna(), M.segmentation.dropna()).statistic, 3) for c in M if c != "segmentation"})

Distribution distance to the segmentation (two-sample KS statistic), P1 a, P4 b: {'polynomial': np.float64(0.207), 'ellipse': np.float64(0.42), 'spline': np.float64(0.346), 'annulus': np.float64(0.272)}

Result: partially reproduced. The polynomial fit is the closest model for the largest share of cross sections in every one of the 96 combinations: 81.4 to 85.7% against the three fits, and 52.8 to 76.5% when the annulus competes. No combination puts all four peaks within tolerance on linear bins, which the criterion uses: at most 2 (for example P1 a, P4 b, erosion 3, P5 a, outliers out: polynomial 8.48e14, ellipse 3.9e14, spline 1.15e16 and annulus 1.35e15, the last two within). On logarithmic bins, a variant the claims file names for fig6b but not for this claim, two combinations put all four within (P1 a, P4 b, erosion 5, P5 b, all values: 1.37e15, 7.36e14, 1.08e16 and 1.33e15, with the polynomial closest in 82.3% and 57.9%). By the two-sample KS statistic (P1 a, P4 b, erosion 3) the polynomial distribution is the closest to the segmentation's (0.207), then the annulus (0.272), the spline (0.346) and the ellipse (0.42), so the ellipse is not second, as the statement has it. Median resistances: segmentation 5.28e15, polynomial 3.52e15, annulus 2.56e15, ellipse 1.33e15, spline 1.07e16.

ellipse-annulus-underestimate¶

The resistance distribution of the optimal elliptical annulus is very similar to that of the ellipse fit, and both tend to underestimate the resistance of the segmented PVS.

Readings of "underestimate": (a) the median of the per-cross-section ratio to the segmentation is below 1 for both; (b) the peak and median of both are below the segmentation's. Similarity: the annulus-over-ellipse ratios of the peaks and of the medians within 10% of 1.87 and 1.61.

In [17]:
rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k, p5 in [(k, p5) for k in P6 for p5 in "ab"]:
            M = models(d, p5, k).dropna(subset=["segmentation", "ellipse", "annulus"])
            for p7 in P7:
                for sc in ("linear", "log"):
                    pk = {n: rpeak(M[n], p7, sc) for n in ("segmentation", "ellipse", "annulus")}
                    md_ = {n: M[n].median() for n in pk}
                    ua = (M.ellipse / M.segmentation).median() < 1 and (M.annulus / M.segmentation).median() < 1
                    ub = all(pk[n] < pk["segmentation"] and md_[n] < md_["segmentation"] for n in ("ellipse", "annulus"))
                    rp, rm = pk["annulus"] / pk["ellipse"], md_["annulus"] / md_["ellipse"]
                    sim = within(rp, 1.87, 0.187) and within(rm, 1.61, 0.161)
                    rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P5": p5, "P7": p7, "bins": sc + ("" if sc == "linear" else " (variant)"), "n": len(M),
                                 "med_ratio_ell": round((M.ellipse / M.segmentation).median(), 3),
                                 "med_ratio_ann": round((M.annulus / M.segmentation).median(), 3),
                                 "under_a": ua, "under_b": ub, "ann/ell_peak": round(rp, 3), "ann/ell_median": round(rm, 3),
                                 "similar": sim, "match": (ua or ub) and sim if sc == "linear" else np.nan})
eau = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(eau.to_string(index=False))
lin = eau[eau.bins == "linear"]
lin = eau[eau.bins == "linear"]
print("\nCombinations with the similarity ratios within 10%:")
print(lin[lin.similar].to_string(index=False))
print("Ranges on linear bins: annulus/ellipse peak", lin["ann/ell_peak"].min(), "to", lin["ann/ell_peak"].max(), "; median", lin["ann/ell_median"].min(), "to", lin["ann/ell_median"].max())
print("\nLinear bins, as in fig5b's criterion: combinations with both underestimating (a or b):", int((lin.under_a | lin.under_b).sum()),
      "of", len(lin), "; with the similarity ratios within 10%:", int(lin.similar.sum()))

Result: reproduced. Both the ellipse fit and the annulus underestimate the segmentation in all 48 combinations on linear bins. The annulus-over-ellipse ratios are within 10% of the paper's 1.87 and 1.61 in one of the 48: P1 (b), P4 (a), erosion 1, P5 (b), outliers out, with 1.82 for the peaks and 1.702 for the medians (median per-cross-section ratio 0.348 for the ellipse and 0.58 for the annulus). The criterion's "under one reading" counts it, but the outcome rests on that single combination, under the P4 reading that leaves 4 segments without a cross section. Over all 48 the ratio of the medians is 1.409 to 2.264 and that of the peaks 0.038 to 2.259.

spline-resistance-five-times¶

The spline fit's resistance is considerably larger than the segmentation's, its distribution peak about 5 times larger, despite a larger area ratio, because the spline PVS narrows rapidly away from the vessel.

Ratio of the spline peak to the segmentation peak, with the bins of the claims it depends on: reading (a) 5 within 0.5, (b) 6.2 within 0.62; and the median spline resistance above the median segmented one.

        d = sel(p1, p4)

fig7-velocity-profiles¶

In a representative cross section, the polynomial fit's velocity profile resembles the segmentation's, the ellipse fit gives much higher velocities and the spline fit much lower; these trends are generally consistent across cross sections.

Velocity at 500 Pa/m. Readings: (a) maximum velocity, (b) mean velocity. Holds when in more than half the cross sections the ellipse is faster than the segmentation, the spline slower, and the polynomial closer to the segmentation than either.

rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k, (rd, pre) in [(k, r) for k in P6 for r in (("a", "umax"), ("b", "umean"))]:
            u = pd.DataFrame({m: d[f"{pre}_{s}"] for m, s in (("seg", "seg"), ("ell", f"ell_e{k}"), ("spl", f"spl_e{k}"), ("pol", f"pol_e{k}"))}).dropna()
            fe = 100 * (u.ell > u.seg).mean(); ss = 100 * (u.spl < u.seg).mean()
            dp = (u.pol - u.seg).abs()
            pc = 100 * ((dp < (u.ell - u.seg).abs()) & (dp < (u.spl - u.seg).abs())).mean()
            rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "reading": rd, "n": len(u), "ellipse_faster_pct": round(fe, 1),
                         "spline_slower_pct": round(ss, 1), "polynomial_closest_pct": round(pc, 1),
                         "median_seg_um_s": round(1e6 * u.seg.median(), 2), "median_ell": round(1e6 * u.ell.median(), 2),
                         "median_spl": round(1e6 * u.spl.median(), 2), "median_pol": round(1e6 * u.pol.median(), 2),

fig8-ellipse-parameters¶

The ellipse fit shows an elongated, eccentric PVS with the vessel slightly below its center; R1 peaks at 28 um and R3 at 35 um, R3/R1 at 0.80, R2/R1 at 2.89, R3/R2 at 0.398, the vertical offset Ov at 0.24, and the horizontal offset Oh is centered near zero with a much wider distribution than Ov.

R2 and R3 are the semi-axes of the ellipse fit to the PVS and vessel together, holes filled (P9, as amended after the question on this claim). Offsets in units of (a) R1, (b) R3, (c) um; Ov positive when the vessel is below the ellipse center. Oh conditions: median within one Ov peak of zero, IQR of Oh at least twice that of Ov.

        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            r1, r2, r3 = d[f"R1_e{k}"], d[f"R2_e{k}"], d[f"R3_e{k}"]
            for unit in "abc":
                den = r1 if unit == "a" else (r3 if unit == "b" else 1.0)
                ov, oh = (d[f"Ov_e{k}"] / den).dropna(), (d[f"Oh_e{k}"] / den).dropna()
                for p7 in P7:
                    v = {"R3": pvs.peak(r3.dropna(), p7), "R3/R1": pvs.peak((r3 / r1).dropna(), p7), "R2/R1": pvs.peak((r2 / r1).dropna(), p7),
                         "R3/R2": pvs.peak((r3 / r2).dropna(), p7), "Ov": pvs.peak(ov, p7)}
                    oh_c = abs(oh.median()) <= abs(v["Ov"])
                    oh_w = (oh.quantile(0.75) - oh.quantile(0.25)) >= 2 * (ov.quantile(0.75) - ov.quantile(0.25))
                    okv = {n: within(v[n], e, t) for n, e, t in EXP_8}
                    rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "units": unit, "P7": p7, **{n: round(x, 3) for n, x in v.items()},
                                 "Oh_median": round(oh.median(), 3), "Oh_IQR": round(oh.quantile(0.75) - oh.quantile(0.25), 3),
                                 "Ov_IQR": round(ov.quantile(0.75) - ov.quantile(0.25), 3), "Oh_centered": oh_c, "Oh_wider": oh_w,
                                 "n_within": sum(okv.values()), "match": all(okv.values()) and oh_c and oh_w,
                                 "ratios_within": okv["R3/R1"] and okv["R2/R1"] and okv["R3/R2"]})
f8 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f8.to_string(index=False))
print("\nCombinations matching:", int(f8.match.sum()), "; with the three ratios within tolerance:", int(f8.ratios_within.sum()), "of", len(f8))
print("Ranges over all combinations:", {n: (f8[n].min(), f8[n].max()) for n, _, _ in EXP_8},
      "; within tolerance in:", {n: int(sum(within(v, e, t) for v in f8[n])) for n, e, t in EXP_8})
print("\nThe 8 combinations with the most values within tolerance (compact):")
print(f8.sort_values("n_within", ascending=False).head(8)[["P1", "P4", "P6", "units", "P7", "R3", "R3/R1", "R2/R1", "R3/R2", "Ov", "Oh_centered", "Oh_wider", "n_within"]].to_string(index=False))
d = sel("a", "b")
print("\nVariant, not used by the criterion since the answer: ellipse of the PVS alone (P1 a, P4 b, P7 b): R3 peak",

R3 peaks at 27.35 to 30.10 um (expected 35 within 3.5) and R3/R1 at 0.965 to 1.107 (expected 0.80 within 0.08), within tolerance in no combination; R2/R1 (2.636 to 3.181) is within in 69 of 72 combinations and R3/R2 (0.347 to 0.437) in 54 of 72. Ov is within tolerance of 0.24 in 5 of 72. The IQR of Oh is at least twice that of Ov in all 72, and the median of Oh lies within one Ov peak of zero in 11. The ellipse of the PVS alone, the variant above, gives R3 19.8 um and R3/R1 0.667.

fig9c-pvs-two-lobes¶

The PVS usually consists of two mostly or entirely disconnected lobes on either side of the vessel; the polynomial fit's HC (top of PVS above top of vessel) peaks at zero, and when the lobes connect the channel is narrow, usually less than 0.5 R1.

Peak of HC/R1 within 0.1 of zero (the claims file's tolerance), and, among cross sections with HC above zero, more than half with HC below 0.5 R1.

In [22]:
rows = []

    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            hc = (d[f"HC_e{k}"] / d[f"R1_e{k}"]).dropna()
            pos = hc[hc > 0]
            for p7 in P7:
                pk = pvs.peak(hc, p7)
                rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P7": p7, "n": len(hc), "peak_HC/R1": round(pk, 3),

fig9e-pvs-width-asymmetry¶

The PVS is about twice as wide as the vessel radius and asymmetric about the vessel; the short-side width WS/R1 peaks near 1.1, the long-side width WL/R1 near 1.9, and WS/WL near 0.5.

WS and WL are the shorter and longer of the two side widths of the polynomial fit (vessel edge to PVS end). Peaks within 0.108, 0.185 and 0.0502 of 1.08, 1.85 and 0.502.

In [23]:
def widths(d, k):
    w = d[[f"WL_e{k}", f"WR_e{k}"]].values  # left and right side widths
    return pd.DataFrame({"WS": np.nanmin(w, 1), "WL": np.nanmax(w, 1), "R1": d[f"R1_e{k}"].values,
                         "left": w[:, 0], "right": w[:, 1], "location": d.location.values}).dropna()


rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            w = widths(d, k)
            for p7 in P7:
                v = {"WS/R1": pvs.peak(w.WS / w.R1, p7), "WL/R1": pvs.peak(w.WL / w.R1, p7), "WS/WL": pvs.peak(w.WS / w.WL, p7)}
                rows.append({"P1": p1, "P4": p4, "P6": k, "P7": p7, "n": len(w), **{n: round(x, 3) for n, x in v.items()},
                             "median_WS/R1": round((w.WS / w.R1).median(), 3), "median_WL/R1": round((w.WL / w.R1).median(), 3),
                             "median_WS/WL": round((w.WS / w.WL).median(), 3),
                             "match": within(v["WS/R1"], 1.08, 0.108) and within(v["WL/R1"], 1.85, 0.185) and within(v["WS/WL"], 0.502, 0.0502)})
f9e = pd.DataFrame(rows)

left-right-no-difference¶

The PVS widths on the left and right sides of the vessel do not differ significantly.

Readings: (a) Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired left and right widths over all cross sections; (b) two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; (c) Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the per-segment median widths (14 pairs); alpha 0.05. Left and right are fixed by the direction along the centerline.

In [24]:

    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            w = widths(d, k)
            pa = stats.wilcoxon(w.left, w.right).pvalue
            pb = stats.ks_2samp(w.left, w.right).pvalue
            m = w.groupby("location")[["left", "right"]].median()
            pc = stats.wilcoxon(m.left, m.right).pvalue

Result: blocked (methods underspecified). The readings disagree in every combination: the paired Wilcoxon test (a) and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (b) find a difference (p 2e-30 to 8e-190 and 1e-31 to 2e-142; median left minus right -9.6 to -18.0 um), while the Wilcoxon test on the per-segment medians (c) does not (p 0.055 to 0.715). Readings (a) and (b) treat thousands of neighbouring cross sections, which are not independent, as independent samples, so their p-values overstate the evidence; reading (c) has independent units. The criterion sends the split to methods_underspecified. Left and right differ by segment in both directions (left wider in B, C, E, F, L, M and N; right wider in A, D, G, H, I, J and K).

fig9a-heights-taper¶

The PVS is tallest next to the vessel and narrows far from it; the heights H1/R1, H2/R1 and H3/R1 peak at 1.34, 0.792 and 0.307, so H1 is about 4 times H3.

Heights of the polynomial fit over R1, (a) both sides pooled, (b) the mean of the two sides.

In [25]:
def heights(d, k, rd):
    r1 = d[f"R1_e{k}"]
    if rd == "a":
        return pd.DataFrame({h: np.r_[d[f"{h}L_e{k}"] / r1, d[f"{h}R_e{k}"] / r1] for h in ("H1", "H2", "H3")}).dropna()
    return pd.DataFrame({h: (d[f"{h}L_e{k}"] + d[f"{h}R_e{k}"]) / 2 / r1 for h in ("H1", "H2", "H3")}).dropna()

One of the 48 combinations puts the three peaks within tolerance: P1 (b), P4 (b), erosion 3, both sides pooled and outliers out, with H1/R1 1.228, H2/R1 0.820 and H3/R1 0.305 (expected 1.34, 0.792 and 0.307). The outcome rests on that one combination; in the others the H1/R1 peak runs from 0.343 to 1.445. The order H1 above H2 above H3 holds for the peaks and the medians in 12 of 48 combinations. The medians are H1/R1 1.037 to 1.199, H2/R1 1.108 to 1.205 and H3/R1 0.458 to 0.536, so by median H1 is about 2.3 times H3, not 4, and with P4 (a) H2 is above H1.

fig9f-pvs-concave¶

The bottom edge of the PVS is most often concave; the distribution of (H2 - H3)/(H1 - H2) peaks at 0.108, below the value of 1 that separates concave from convex.

As fig9a, with the same readings: (a) the ratio per side, both sides pooled; (b) the ratio of the mean heights of the two sides. Peak within 0.0108 of 0.108 and more than half the values below 1.

rows = []
for p1 in TARGET:
    for p4 in P4:
        d = sel(p1, p4)
        for k in P6:
            for rd in "ab":
                if rd == "a":
                    c = pd.Series(np.r_[(d[f"H2L_e{k}"] - d[f"H3L_e{k}"]) / (d[f"H1L_e{k}"] - d[f"H2L_e{k}"]),
                                        (d[f"H2R_e{k}"] - d[f"H3R_e{k}"]) / (d[f"H1R_e{k}"] - d[f"H2R_e{k}"])])
                else:
                    h = heights(d, k, "b")
                    c = (h.H2 - h.H3) / (h.H1 - h.H2)

Result: partially reproduced. More than half the values are below 1 in every combination (63.9 to 73.6%; medians -0.627 to 0.465), so the bottom edge is most often concave. The peak is within 0.0108 of 0.108 in no combination; with outliers out it is 0.164 to 1.162, and over all values the bins are stretched by extreme ratios (down to -4.03e4 and up to 1.06e6) where H1 is close to H2.

Sensitivity to location E¶

The cleaned path of E follows a side branch of the vessel network in its mask (data check), and its PVS lobes are only 29 to 52% of the slice's PVS. E is one of the paper's 14 segments, so every claim keeps it. The cell below computes each claim's table again without E and counts, for each column the outcome rests on, the combinations that meet it with and without E.

In [27]:

Location E. Without E most of the counts the outcomes rest on do not change. Those that move: fig8's three ratios are within tolerance in 12 of 72 combinations in place of none, which would meet its partial rule; fig9a loses its one matching combination, while the order H1 above H2 above H3 (its partial rule) holds in 11 of 48; fig5d keeps 1 matching combination of the 4; vessel-radius-peak holds in 9 of 24 in place of 13, spline-resistance-five-times in 18 of 48 (both bin scales) in place of 15, the partial rule of table2 in 18 of 96 in place of 24 and that of fig6a in 3 of 8 in place of 2. Without E the fewest cross sections at 0.648 um (P4 b) is 409 and the most still 604. The readings of left-right-no-difference still split in every combination (p of reading c 0.055 to 0.414). So fig8-ellipse-parameters and fig9a-heights-taper depend on E: without it both would be partially reproduced. E is one of the paper's 14 segments, but its cross sections here are of a side branch, not of the artery the paper measured, so neither keeping nor dropping it gives the paper's E. The outcomes keep E, as the claims file's 14 segments do, and the record states the dependence.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. It starts from the deposited segmentations. The centerline is skimage's 3D thinning, not MATLAB's bwskel with manual removal of points; the longest path through the skeleton, cleaned of points farther from the polynomial fit than the vessel radius and of points that revisit a stretch already passed, stands in for the manual cleaning. Cross sections are sampled by linear interpolation of the masks, not with obliqueslice, and their PVS is the two largest PVS regions within one vessel radius of the vessel. Planes that the PVS mask fills edge to edge (E and F) are cleared. Pixels in both masks are counted as vessel. The resistance is solved by finite differences on the pixel grid, not by finite elements. Reading (b) of P2 is run for the counts only. Every other reading of the claims file is run, and the tables show each. The ellipse is fit to the PVS and vessel together, holes filled, as the claims file has it since a reader answered the question on fig8-ellipse-parameters. These choices changed five outcomes after the first verification (see the attempt record). After the second verification no outcome changed. The data check now shows how far the cleaned path meanders; counts estimated for a path along the fitted centerline fall inside the criterion's range, and a change of cross-section-counts to reproduced was proposed. The third verification did not agree, since no slices were taken along such a path and its step was not measured, so the outcome stays not reproduced. Location E, whose cleaned path follows a side branch, is kept; the outcomes of fig8-ellipse-parameters and fig9a-heights-taper would both be partially reproduced without it.

What was found about the dataset. The earlier published version lacks the PVS masks of L, M and N. The deposited vessel and PVS masks overlap in 11 of 14 files (up to 344565 voxels at E), though the Methods say overlaps were removed. At E and F the PVS mask fills every plane below a depth (87 and 58 planes). The vessel mask of E holds a network of branching vessels, though the Methods say branches were removed by hand. L, M and N state a depth step of 0.648 um while their session descriptions say 1 um; round vessel cross sections are consistent with the stated 0.648 um. The emission wavelengths put 698 nm on the vessel channel (FITC-dextran), which the Methods give as 525 nm. The 2D time series used to validate the segmentation are not in the dandiset.
